sections.heading: What is the In-Place Linked List Reversal Pattern?
sections.content: This pattern reverses all or part of a linked list by changing the next pointers of the existing nodes, without creating new nodes or using extra memory. You walk through the list once and, at each node, point it backward instead of forward. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, and it is the building block for many harder list problems.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Reverse a whole linked list
Reverse a sublist between positions left and right
Reverse nodes in groups of K
Reverse every alternating group of K nodes
Rotate a list
Check if a list is a palindrome (reverse the second half)
Reorder a list or add two numbers stored in reverse
You are told not to use extra space or not to change node values

sections.heading: Linked List Node Definition
The Three Pointer Idea
sections.content: Keep three references: prev (the already reversed part), curr (the node you are working on) and next (saved so you do not lose the rest of the list). At each step: save curr.next, point curr.next to prev, then move prev and curr one step forward. When curr becomes null, prev is the new head.

Template 3: Reverse a Sublist (Positions left to right)
sections.code:
fun reverseBetween(head: ListNode?, left: Int, right: Int): ListNode? {
    if (head == null || left == right) return head
    val dummy = ListNode(0)
    dummy.next = head
    var before: ListNode = dummy
    repeat(left - 1) { before = before.next!! }   // node just before the sublist

    val start = before.next!!                      // first node of the sublist
    var prev: ListNode? = null
    var curr: ListNode? = start
    repeat(right - left + 1) {
        val next = curr!!.next
        curr!!.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = next
    }
    before.next = prev          // connect to the new start of the sublist
    start.next = curr           // connect the old start (now the tail) to the rest
    return dummy.next
}
// Time: O(n)   Space: O(1)

sections.heading: Why Use a Dummy Node
sections.content: A dummy node placed before the head removes special cases. If the reversal starts at position 1, the real head changes. With a dummy, 'the node before the sublist' always exists, and you can simply return dummy.next at the end.

Example 6: Add Two Numbers (Digits in Reverse Order)
sections.code:
fun addTwoNumbers(l1: ListNode?, l2: ListNode?): ListNode? {
    val dummy = ListNode(0)
    var tail = dummy
    var a = l1
    var b = l2
    var carry = 0
    while (a != null || b != null || carry != 0) {
        val sum = (a?.`val` ?: 0) + (b?.`val` ?: 0) + carry
        carry = sum / 10
        tail.next = ListNode(sum % 10)
        tail = tail.next!!
        a = a?.next
        b = b?.next
    }
    return dummy.next
}
// Time: O(max(n, m))   Space: O(1) extra (output not counted)

sections.heading: Example 7: Add Two Numbers II (Digits in Forward Order)
Example 7b: Palindrome Linked List
sections.code:
fun isPalindrome(head: ListNode?): Boolean {
    var slow = head
    var fast = head
    while (fast?.next != null) {           // find the middle
        slow = slow!!.next
        fast = fast.next!!.next
    }
    var prev: ListNode? = null             // reverse the second half
    var curr = slow
    while (curr != null) {
        val next = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = next
    }
    var left = head
    var right = prev
    while (right != null) {                // compare both halves
        if (left!!.`val` != right.`val`) return false
        left = left.next
        right = right.next
    }
    return true
}
// Time: O(n)   Space: O(1)

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Not saving curr.next before overwriting it, which loses the rest of the list
Returning curr instead of prev (curr is null when the loop ends)
Forgetting to reconnect the reversed sublist to the nodes before and after it
Not setting the old head's next to null, which creates a cycle
Skipping the dummy node, which makes reversing from position 1 messy
Reversing the last group in K-group when it has fewer than K nodes
Forgetting the empty list and single-node cases
Using the recursive version on very long lists, which can cause a stack overflow

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Reverse a list with three pointers: prev, curr and next
Always save curr.next before changing it
When the loop ends, prev is the new head
For partial reversals, track the node before the sublist and reconnect both ends
Use a dummy node to avoid special cases at the head
The iterative version is O(1) space, while the recursive and stack versions use O(n)
